Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

## Local Chrome

The default daemon can keep many tabs and visit many sites; browser-use has
no per-site, screenshot, or result-count limit that requires a new daemon.

                                      Validity of the Training-Load Concept
                          Louis Passﬁeld, Juan M. Murias, Massimo Sacchetti, and Andrea Nicolò

     Training load (TL) is a widely used concept in training prescription and monitoring and is also recognized as as an important tool
     for avoiding athlete injury, illness, and overtraining. With the widespread adoption of wearable devices, TL metrics are used
     increasingly by researchers and practitioners worldwide. Conceptually, TL was proposed as a means to quantify a dose of training
     and used to predict its resulting training effect. However, TL has never been validated as a measure of training dose, and there is a
     risk that fundamental problems related to its calculation are preventing advances in training prescription and monitoring.
     Speciﬁcally, we highlight recent studies from our research groups where we compare the acute performance decrement measured
     following a session with its TL metrics. These studies suggest that most TL metrics are not consistent with their notional training
     dose and that the exercise duration confounds their calculation. These studies also show that total work done is not an appropriate
     way to compare training interventions that differ in duration and intensity. We encourage scientists and practitioners to critically
     evaluate the validity of current TL metrics and suggest that new TL metrics need to be developed.

                                      Validity of the Training-Load Concept
                          Louis Passﬁeld, Juan M. Murias, Massimo Sacchetti, and Andrea Nicolò

     Training load (TL) is a widely used concept in training prescription and monitoring and is also recognized as as an important tool
     for avoiding athlete injury, illness, and overtraining. With the widespread adoption of wearable devices, TL metrics are used
     increasingly by researchers and practitioners worldwide. Conceptually, TL was proposed as a means to quantify a dose of training
     and used to predict its resulting training effect. However, TL has never been validated as a measure of training dose, and there is a
     risk that fundamental problems related to its calculation are preventing advances in training prescription and monitoring.
     Speciﬁcally, we highlight recent studies from our research groups where we compare the acute performance decrement measured
     following a session with its TL metrics. These studies suggest that most TL metrics are not consistent with their notional training
     dose and that the exercise duration confounds their calculation. These studies also show that total work done is not an appropriate
     way to compare training interventions that differ in duration and intensity. We encourage scientists and practitioners to critically
     evaluate the validity of current TL metrics and suggest that new TL metrics need to be developed.

     Keywords: athletic training, endurance training, exercise performance, exercise physiology, exercise training

 exercise and load combination compared with the mean and peak system velocities produced. Barbell and system velocity are
 distinct characteristics that should not be substituted for one another. Owing to the characteristics of the transition phase, mean
 barbell and system velocity may not provide strength and conditioning practitioners with meaningful information related to load
 prescription.

Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on
neuromuscular performance and hormonal response
Abstract
This study aimed to compare the effects of two resistance training (RT) programs with
different velocity losses allowed in each set: 10% (VL10%) vs. 30% (VL30%) on
neuromuscular performance and hormonal response. Twenty-five young healthy males
were randomly assigned into two groups: VL10% (n=12) or VL30% (n=13). Subjects
followed a velocity-based RT program for 8 weeks (2 sessions per week) using only the
full-squat (SQ) exercise at 70-85% 1RM. Repetition velocity was recorded in all
training sessions. A 20-m running sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), 1RM, muscle
endurance and EMG during SQ exercise, and resting hormonal concentrations were
assessed before and after RT program. Both groups showed similar improvements in
For personal use only. This Just-IN manuscript is the accepted manuscript prior to copy editing and page composition. It may differ from the final official version of record.
muscle strength and endurance variables (VL10%: 7.0-74.8%; VL30%: 4.2-73.2%).
The VL10% resulted in greater percentage increments in CMJ (9.2% vs. 5.4%) and
sprint performance (-1.5% vs. 0.4%) than VL30%, despite VL10% performed less than
half of the repetitions than VL30% during RT. In addition, only VL10% showed slight
increments in EMG variables, whereas no significant changes in resting hormonal
concentrations were observed. Therefore, our results suggest that velocity losses in the
set as low as 10% are enough to achieve significant improvements in neuromuscular
performance, which means greater efficiency during RT.
Novelty bullets
 The VL10% group showed similar or even greater percentage of changes in physical
performance compared to VL30%.
3
  Page 4 of 47
 No significant changes in resting hormonal concentrations were observed for any
training group.
 Curvilinear relationships between percentage VL in the set and changes in strength
and CMJ performance were observed.
Key words: muscle adaptations, full squat, physical performance, resistance training,
EMG, muscle strength, endocrine response.

IKDC questionnaire score improved from 6 to 9 months (F = 19.3, p < 0.001, ES = 0.47).

   "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000002295",
   "abstract":"The study compared four 8-week resistance training programmes with velocity loss thresholds of 0%, 10%, 20% and 40% in each set, using the full squat. Outcomes included muscle hypertrophy and architecture, tensiomyography, sprint, jump, isometric strength, a progressive loading test and fatigue. No between-group differences were found for sprint, jump or strength gains despite different total volumes. Higher thresholds (20% and 40%) maximised hypertrophy, but the 40% threshold also produced negative neuromuscular changes.",
   "tldr":"Higher velocity loss thresholds gave more muscle growth in this study, but the largest threshold also hurt some neuromuscular measures. Moderate thresholds look like the sensible middle ground for strength and neuromuscular gains.",

   "findings":"No between-group differences in sprint, jump or strength gains. VL20 and VL40 showed significant within-group increases in muscle hypertrophy (P < 0.001), but the group-time interaction was P = 0.06. Only VL40 showed a slower delay time in the vastus lateralis (group-time interaction P = 0.05) and a decrease in early rate of force development (P = 0.04).",
   "limitations":"Only one exercise and one 8-week programme were studied, in men who were resistance-trained and physically active rather than sport-specific athletes. The hypertrophy group interaction was not significant at P < 0.05.",
   "practicalImplications":"Moderate velocity loss thresholds appear to balance strength and muscle gains against negative neuromuscular effects in this population. Very high thresholds such as 40% may add fatigue-related neuromuscular costs without extra strength gain.",
   "athleteDev":"For squat-based strength blocks, set a moderate velocity loss threshold rather than training to near-failure every set. Use the threshold to limit fatigue, and expect strength and sprint gains to be similar across thresholds in this sample.",
   "rtp":"The study was in healthy resistance-trained men and did not test injured athletes. It cannot be used to guide return-to-sport loading decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q45",
 "sourceFile":"Velocity loss as a variable for    monitoring resistance exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'Velocity Loss as a Variable for Monitoring Resistance Exercise' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Study I tested 22 young healthy men to failure on the bench press against eight loads from 50% to 85% 1RM, and found a very close relationship between relative velocity loss and the percentage of repetitions performed. This relationship was similar for 50-70% 1RM and progressively greater at 75-85% 1RM. Study II tested 28 physically active sport science students on two maximum-repetition tests at 60% 1RM, with a coefficient of variation of 2.7-12.1% for the percentage of repetitions performed, depending on the velocity loss. The authors provide prediction equations from velocity loss to the percentage of repetitions performed.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only the bench press was tested, in young men with estimated rather than directly tested 1RM. The reliability was not at the authors' 10% CV criterion at every velocity loss level, so the prediction equations are best seen as estimates.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could apply the prediction equations to any lift, athlete or load, but they were derived from bench press repetitions in young men.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"González-Badillo JJ, Yañez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, Rodríguez-Rosell D. Velocity Loss as a Variable for Monitoring Resistance Exercise. Int J Sports Med. 2017;38:217-225.",
   "doi":"10.1055/s-0042-120324",
   "abstract":"The study analysed the pattern of repetition velocity decline during a set to failure against submaximal bench press loads from 50% to 85% 1RM, and the reliability of the percentage of repetitions performed for a given velocity loss. Velocity loss tracked the percentage of repetitions performed very closely across loads, especially at 50-70% 1RM. The percentage of repetitions for a given velocity loss showed high absolute reliability, and prediction equations are provided.",
   "tldr":"Velocity loss within a set predicts how many repetitions a lifter has left in the tank on the bench press. It is a useful monitoring tool, but the equations are estimates and were built on bench press data.",
   "methods":"Study I: 22 young healthy men performed eight maximum-repetition tests to failure at 50-85% 1RM in random order, one week apart. Study II: 28 physically active sport science students performed two maximum-repetition tests at 60% 1RM. Repetition velocity was measured with a linear transducer.",
   "findings":"In Study I, velocity loss and the percentage of repetitions performed were closely related for all loads, similar for 50-70% 1RM and progressively greater for 75-85% 1RM. In Study II, the coefficient of variation for the percentage of repetitions performed ranged from 2.7% to 12.1%, depending on the velocity loss.",
   "limitations":"Only the bench press was tested. The 1RM was estimated from load-velocity relationships in young men. The reliability was above the authors' 10% CV criterion at some velocity loss levels.",
   "practicalImplications":"Monitoring repetition velocity during a bench press set can estimate how many repetitions remain in reserve. Use the authors' equations as approximate guides for bench press sets rather than exact counts.",
   "athleteDev":"Use velocity loss to set bench press set endpoints, for example stopping at a chosen velocity loss rather than a fixed repetition count. Expect the estimate of repetitions remaining to be approximate.",
   "rtp":"The study tested healthy men on the bench press and did not include injured athletes or return-to-sport tasks. It cannot be used to judge readiness after injury."
 }
}

 "paper":{
   "year":null,
   "citation":"Rodríguez-Rosell D, Yáñez-García JM, Mora-Custodio R, et al. Velocity-based resistance training: Impact of velocity loss in the set on neuromuscular performance and hormonal response. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. Accepted manuscript; year, volume and pages not printed.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"The study compared two velocity-based resistance training programmes with 10% and 30% velocity loss in each set, using the full squat in 25 young healthy men over 8 weeks. Strength and endurance improved similarly in both groups. The 10% group showed greater gains in countermovement jump and sprint performance despite performing fewer than half the repetitions, and resting hormone concentrations did not change.",
   "tldr":"A 10% velocity loss threshold gave jump and sprint gains similar to or better than a 30% threshold, with far fewer squat repetitions. Hormones did not change in either group.",
   "methods":"Twenty-five healthy young men were matched on estimated 1RM and randomised to VL10% (n = 12) or VL30% (n = 13). Both trained the full squat twice weekly for 8 weeks at 70-85% 1RM, with repetition velocity recorded in every session. Sprint, countermovement jump, 1RM, muscle endurance, EMG during the squat and resting hormones were tested before and after training.",
   "findings":"Both groups improved strength and endurance measures to similar extents (VL10%: 7.0-74.8%; VL30%: 4.2-73.2%). VL10% showed greater percentage increases in countermovement jump (9.2% vs 5.4%) and sprint performance (-1.5% vs 0.4%, as reported). Only VL10% showed slight increases in EMG variables, and no significant changes in resting hormone concentrations were observed.",
   "limitations":"Small groups, one exercise and an 8-week intervention in physically active sport science students. The reported group comparisons are percentage changes, and the abstract does not give between-group test statistics.",
   "practicalImplications":"A 10% velocity loss threshold can produce strength and jump gains with far fewer squat repetitions than a 30% threshold in recreationally trained men. Use it as a way to reduce training volume without giving up the main gains, while noting the small sample.",
   "athleteDev":"For squat-based strength blocks, a tight velocity loss limit may give similar strength gains with lower total volume. Use velocity loss to end sets early, and track jump and sprint measures alongside strength.",
   "rtp":"The study tested healthy recreational men and did not include injured athletes or return-to-sport tasks. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport loading or readiness criteria."
 }
}

 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the persisting jump deficits as proof that jump impulse should drive return-to-sport decisions, but the study only describes changes between 6 and 9 months and does not test any return-to-sport criterion.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Costley JAE, Miles JJ, King E, Daniels KAJ. Vertical jump impulse deficits persist from six to nine months after ACL reconstruction. Sports Biomech. 2021.",
   "doi":"10.1080/14763141.2021.1945137",
   "abstract":"The study aimed to evaluate countermovement jump phase-specific impulse and isokinetic strength inter-limb asymmetry from 6 to 9 months after ACL reconstruction in 44 male athletes, and to examine whether changes in strength asymmetry explained changes in impulse asymmetry. Strength asymmetry improved mainly through better performance of the reconstructed limb. Concentric impulse asymmetry reduced, while changes in strength asymmetry explained little of the impulse change. Graft type did not modulate the findings.",
   "tldr":"Jump impulse and strength asymmetries are still present at 9 months after ACL reconstruction, though some improve. Strength gains alone do not explain the jump changes, so jump impulse deserves its own attention in late rehabilitation.",
   "methods":"Forty-four male athletes with hamstring or bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts were tested 6 and 9 months after ACL reconstruction. Countermovement jump phase-specific impulse and knee isokinetic flexor and extensor strength were measured for both limbs. Two-way mixed-model ANOVAs compared sessions and graft types, and linear regression assessed the link between impulse and strength asymmetry changes.",
   "findings":"Knee extension and flexion strength asymmetry improved from 6 to 9 months (extension ES -0.50; flexion ES -0.37). Only the concentric phase of the countermovement jump showed a significant reduction in impulse asymmetry (ES -0.42). No significant change was found in eccentric deceleration asymmetry.    "limitations":"The design is observational with two time points and no control group. The sport and competition level are not stated. The abstract's report of bilateral decreases in eccentric deceleration impulse does not match the asymmetry results, which show no significant change in eccentric asymmetry.",
   "practicalImplications":"Check jump impulse asymmetry, not just jump height, in later-stage rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction. Do not assume that improving knee strength asymmetry will fix jump impulse asymmetry.",
   "athleteDev":"After ACL reconstruction, track countermovement jump impulse asymmetry alongside strength asymmetry, and include concentric jump work in the plan, since concentric impulse asymmetry was the measure that changed.",
   "rtp":"The paper shows that jump impulse and strength asymmetries persist at 9 months after ACL reconstruction. It supports including jump impulse in later-stage return-to-sport testing, but it does not set a passing threshold or show that these measures predict re-injury or return to sport."
 }
}

Changes in absolute isokinetic strength and phase-specific impulse of independent
ACLR and uninvolved limbs from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR
Absolute values of independent limbs (ACLR/uninvolved) at 6- and 9-month testing
sessions are displayed in Table 1 with results of the mixed-model ANOVA presented in
Table 2.
 From 6 to 9 months post-operatively, the ACLR limb displayed increases in extensor
and flexor peak torque (F = 17.25–10.66; p < 0.001–0.002) yet uninvolved limb strength
did not significantly change. A main effect of graft was observed within peak extensor
torque of the ACLR-limb, with greater extensor strength displayed by HT-ACLR than
BPTB-ACLR individuals (F = 5.67; p = 0.022). Reductions in eccentric deceleration
impulse were apparent in both the ACLR (F = 8.03; p = 0.007) and uninvolved limb
(F = 13.41; p = 0.001). A main effect of graft on phase-specific impulse was only observed
in the ACLR limb with higher eccentric deceleration impulse in HT (F = 5.63; p = 0.022).
A significant reduction in concentric phase impulse occurred within the uninvolved limb
(F = 6.92; p = 0.012). Neither limb exhibited changes in landing impulse over time. No
interaction effects (time*graft) were found for any isokinetic strength measure, nor in any
CMJ phase, for either limb.
